questions.title: Can a Minnesota employee recover 'average daily wage penalties' under MPWA §181.101, or is that authority solely with the state commissioner?
questions.question_body: In the opinion it is held that penalties may be imposed only if the Minnesota Commissioner serves a demand for payment of wages and, if payment is not made, is authorized to charge and collect a penalty that must be paid to the employee. The court therefore declined to allow Cohen to recover such penalties in federal court. My confusion lies in whether the statute actually gives employees a direct right to litigate penalties, or whether the only available avenue is through the Commissioner. Why does the language of §181.101 make the employment of the Commissioner necessary, and how does that affect a plaintiff’s ability to recover penalties under the MPWA?

questions.title: Federal standing to recover MFLSA statutory penalties when they are payable to the commissioner
questions.question_body: The MFLSA provides for statutory civil penalties that are payable to the U.S. Commissioner, not directly to the employee. The court noted that the plaintiff’s ability to enforce such penalties raises a standing issue, citing *Friends of the Earth v. Laidlaw*. In that case, the penalties were paid to the federal government. Does the same doctrine apply to state‑level statutes like the MFLSA? Can a plaintiff in a federal action still recover statutory penalties that are earmarked for the Commissioner while the money does not go directly to them? How does standing thus shape the plaintiff’s remedy under the MFLSA?

questions.title: Has Minnesota’s Wage Theft Act provided for civil penalties under §181.032(f)(d)(4), and how can an employee enforce them?
questions.question_body: Cohen’s claim under the MWTA is dismissed by the appellate court for lack of argument. I am unclear whether the MWTA actually allows for civil penalties at all. If it does, the statute would presumably require the Commissioner to collect and pay them; if not, it might only allow notice or wage recovery. How should I interpret §181.032(f)(d)(4) in light of the MWTA’s provisions? Is there a statutory basis for an employee to claim penalties, and if so, who is responsible for collecting and distributing those penalties?

questions.title: What procedural hurdles must a plaintiff face when raising new injunctive relief after a summary judgment motion has been filed?
questions.question_body: Cohen attempted to seek an injunction to rescind Consilio’s overtime policy after the district court had granted summary judgment on the prior claims. The opinion references *InfoDeli* and Rule 15 to explain why the court considered this improper. I’m confused about the procedural rules governing new claims after a summary judgment motion. According to the rules, must Cohen amend his complaint to include the injunctive relief? What is the court’s justification for treating the new relief as a separate claim, and can it be effectively pursued after a summary judgment has been granted?

questions.title: How does a change in an employer’s overtime policy affect the availability of penalties and the mootness of civil claims?
questions.question_body: The court vacated the district court’s summary judgment on Cohen’s MFLSA claim, citing the possible mootness of the penalty claim if Consilio’s policy was no longer in place. However, a policy change was enacted in 2019, yet the district court still treated it as if the new policy remained. What factors do courts assess when determining whether a claim is moot, especially regarding the potential for future violations? How does the existence or absence of a specific employment policy influence a court’s jurisdiction over penalties under the MFLSA or the MPWA?

questions.title: How do liquidated damages and statutory penalties differ under the MFLSA, and who is entitled to receive each?
questions.question_body: The opinion notes that Cohen received liquidated damages under the MFLSA but still sought statutory penalties. I am unclear about the statutory language that distinguishes liquidated damages from civil penalties in the MFLSA. Does the statute specify different sources or recipients for these two types of relief? In particular, who is entitled to the money for liquidated damages, and who receives civil penalties? Why might a plaintiff be able to recover one but not the other?

questions.title: What evidentiary standard applies in de novo review of a summary judgment motion, and how does that differ from ordinary appellate review?
questions.question_body: The appellate court reviews the district court’s grant of summary judgment ‘de novo,’ examining the evidence as if it were new. I am trying to understand how this process works and how it differs from an ordinary appellate review, which focuses primarily on legal errors. What evidence must the appellate court consider, and how does the “light most favorable to the nonmoving party” standard influence the outcome? Why does the court re‑examine the facts rather than just test the law?
